scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Wari originates from a pre-Inca agricultural festival called pocoy mita, celebrated in the Huari district of Áncash, Peru.
It was documented in 1570 by Cristóbal de Molina as Waritaki and evolved through Spanish influence, blending indigenous and Christian elements.
The dance is linked to the arrival of rains and religious festivals such as the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and the Virgin of the Rosary.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Wari is performed during religious festivals honoring the Virgin of the Rosary and the Exaltation of the Holy Cross in Huari, as well as occasionally during the Virgin of the Assumption festival in Chacas.
The bells on the knee pads symbolize penitence and devotion to the Cross.
The dance reflects a syncretism of indigenous agricultural rites and Christian celebrations.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Traditionally performed by four dancers and two musicians, the choreography has three main parts: circular formations with rhythmic emphasis on the fourth beat, the arrebato (a light step), and the jaleo or zapateo (a strong stamping step).
In urban areas, groups may include up to eight dancers and a captain.
The dance ends with a zapateo resembling a huayno fugue.
Watch for Arrebato, Jaleo or Zapateo.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music is performed by two cajeros playing the pinkullo flute and the wanqar drum.
The pinkullo is a four-holed wooden flute with a beak mouthpiece, played with the left hand, made from waroma wood.
Listen for the pinkullo flute, wanqar drum.
The pulse is not explicitly described, but rhythmic emphasis on fourth beat suggests a 4/4 pattern.
Music features the piercing, melodic tone of the pinkullo flute combined with the deep, resonant beats of the wanqar drum, creating a rhythmic pattern typical of northern Peruvian highlands.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear formal blue or black suits with white shirts and ties, floral shawls tied over the chest, golden embroidered sashes, and carry handkerchiefs.
The head is covered with a white cloth called uma paño and a pink mesh mask painted with facial features.
They wear white toquilla straw hats decorated with silk ribbons and artificial flowers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: A variant of the original Waritaki exists in Pomabamba province, differing in choreography and musical tempo, performed in Sihuas, Urpay, Taurija, and Pataz in La Libertad region.
Wari descends from pre-Inca agricultural dances, incorporating Spanish colonial elements, especially from Christian festivals, forming a mestizo ritual dance unique to the Huari district.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Wari is a ritual dance performed during religious festivals with symbolic penitential elements such as the heavy bells on knee pads; it should be respected as a devotional practice.
